fields.definition: An LTO (Linear Tape-Open) archive is a long-term backup of session or project data written to Linear Tape-Open magnetic tape cartridges, an open-standard sequential storage format widely used in post-production and broadcast for high-capacity, long-life, low-cost data retention.
fields.plain_english: An LTO archive stores finished projects on magnetic tape for the long haul. Tape is cheap and lasts for years, so studios use it to keep old sessions safe after a job is done.
fields.purpose_function: It provides durable, high-capacity offline storage so completed sessions can be kept for years at a low cost per terabyte and cleared off expensive working drives.
fields.practical_application: An engineer copies a finished session to an LTO cartridge with archiving software, verifies the write, labels the cartridge, and stores it offline as the long-term master backup.
common_mistakes: Assuming a single tape copy is safe, when archives should be verified and ideally duplicated because tapes can fail.
Forgetting that LTO drives read back only a limited number of generations, so very old tapes can become unreadable.
Skipping write verification, so a corrupt archive is not discovered until the data is actually needed.
scenario_contexts: Archiving a completed album's session files after final delivery.
A post house backing up finished film audio to tape for long-term storage.
Freeing studio drive space by moving old projects onto LTO cartridges.

sources: LTO Ultrium technology technical specifications (LTO Program / Consortium)

fields.definition: A metronome, or click track, is a steady audible pulse generated by the DAW at the session tempo, sounding on each beat and often on subdivisions, to give performers and the editor a consistent timing reference.
fields.plain_english: A metronome is a steady beep set to the song's tempo. Musicians play along to it so everything stays in time and lines up neatly.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to keep a performance locked to the project tempo and grid, so recorded parts line up with the bars and beats for editing, quantizing, and overdubbing.
fields.practical_application: Before tracking, the engineer sets the tempo, enables the click, and sends it to the performer's headphones so the take stays on the grid.
common_mistakes: Setting the wrong tempo before recording, so the click fights the performance.
Letting the click bleed into a recording through the wrong output or open headphones near a mic.
Expecting a player to catch the tempo without a count-in to set it first.
scenario_contexts: Recording a drummer to a click so the track can be edited to the grid.
Overdubbing a bass part that must line up with existing tracks.
Tracking to a fixed tempo so parts can be quantized later.

fields.definition: A MIDI articulation map (also called an expression map or articulation set) is a configuration that links a DAW's key-switch or notation commands to the different playing styles of a sampled or virtual instrument, such as legato, staccato, pizzicato, or tremolo, so the correct articulation is triggered during playback.
fields.plain_english: An articulation map tells a sampled instrument which playing style to use, like smooth, short, or plucked. It swaps between those styles for you as the music plays.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to automate switching between an instrument's many playing styles, letting one MIDI track sound realistic without manually reloading patches or memorizing every key switch.
fields.practical_application: A composer assigns articulations in the map so key switches or notation marks automatically call up legato, spiccato, or pizzicato from a large orchestral sample library.
common_mistakes: Building the map for the wrong library, so its key-switch layout does not match and the wrong articulation plays.
Placing key-switch notes in the audible range, so they sound instead of only switching.
Assuming articulation maps transfer between DAWs, when each program uses its own format.
scenario_contexts: Scoring strings that move between legato and staccato phrases.
Setting up a brass library so notation marks trigger the right articulation.
Building an orchestral template that recalls articulations for a full mockup.

sources: Apple Logic Pro User Guide (Articulation Sets)

fields.definition: A MIDI controller lane is an editor sub-track, usually shown beneath the piano roll, that displays and lets you edit continuous controller (CC) data over time, such as modulation (CC1), expression (CC11), sustain (CC64), or pitch bend.
fields.plain_english: A controller lane is a strip under the notes where you draw changes like volume swells or vibrato. It shows those moves as a shape you can edit.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to let an editor view and shape the continuous MIDI messages that add expression and movement to a part, separately from the notes themselves.
fields.practical_application: An editor opens the modulation lane and draws a rising curve to swell a string pad, or fixes sustain-pedal data on a recorded piano in its own lane.
common_mistakes: Confusing MIDI CC lanes with mixer automation, since CC data lives inside the MIDI part, not the track automation.
Editing the wrong CC number, so the intended parameter never moves.
Leaving stray or stuck controller values that carry over and affect later notes.
scenario_contexts: Drawing modulation to add vibrato to a synth lead.
Fixing sustain-pedal data on a recorded piano performance.
Automating expression on an orchestral instrument for a crescendo.

sources: Ableton Live Manual (MIDI note and controller editing)

fields.definition: MIDI editing is the process of viewing and altering recorded or programmed MIDI data, including notes, velocities, timing, and controller messages, within a DAW using tools such as a piano-roll, event list, or score editor.
fields.plain_english: MIDI editing means changing the note data after you record it. You can fix wrong notes, adjust timing, or change how hard each note was hit.
fields.purpose_function: It exists so a performance captured as MIDI can be corrected and shaped after the fact, because MIDI stores playback instructions rather than fixed audio.
fields.practical_application: After recording a keyboard take, the engineer opens the piano roll to fix wrong notes, tighten timing, and adjust velocities before finalizing the part.
common_mistakes: Over-quantizing until the part sounds stiff and loses its feel.
Editing the MIDI but forgetting the virtual instrument patch also shapes the final sound.
Confusing MIDI editing, which changes instructions, with audio editing, which changes a recorded waveform.
scenario_contexts: Cleaning up a programmed drum pattern.
Correcting a few wrong notes in a recorded synth line.
Adjusting note timing and velocity so a part grooves.

sources: Apple Logic Pro User Guide (MIDI editors)

fields.definition: MIDI filtering is the selective blocking or passing of specific MIDI message types, such as aftertouch, pitch bend, program change, or particular controllers, at an input, track, or port so unwanted data is not recorded, transmitted, or played back.
fields.plain_english: MIDI filtering blocks the kinds of MIDI messages you do not want. For example, you can stop extra data like aftertouch from being recorded.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to keep unneeded or problematic MIDI messages out of the data stream, cutting clutter, avoiding conflicts, and saving processing or bandwidth.
fields.practical_application: An engineer switches on an input filter to strip aftertouch from a controller that sends it heavily, keeping the recorded part clean.
common_mistakes: Filtering out a message type you actually need, so expression data goes missing.
Forgetting an input filter is active, then wondering why data will not record.
Confusing input filtering with deleting data already recorded in the part.
scenario_contexts: Blocking noisy aftertouch from a keyboard that oversends it.
Stopping program-change messages from switching patches unexpectedly.
Cleaning a MIDI input so only notes and modulation are recorded.

sources: Steinberg Cubase Operation Manual (MIDI input transformer/filters)

fields.definition: MIDI note editing is the manipulation of individual note events in a MIDI part, changing pitch, start position, length, and velocity, usually in a piano-roll editor.
fields.plain_english: MIDI note editing means changing single notes after recording. You can move a note, make it longer, change its pitch, or set how loud it is.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to correct and refine a MIDI performance note by note, since each MIDI note is a separate, editable event rather than fixed audio.
fields.practical_application: In the piano roll, the engineer drags a flat note up to the right pitch, trims its length, and raises its velocity so it sits in the part.
common_mistakes: Moving a note's pitch when meaning to move its timing, or the reverse.
Overlapping notes on the same pitch, causing stuck or cut-off notes.
Ignoring velocity, so edited notes jump out or disappear in the mix.
scenario_contexts: Fixing a wrong note in a recorded melody.
Tightening the timing of a programmed bassline.
Adjusting note lengths so chords ring or stop cleanly.

fields.definition: MIDI programming is the creation of a musical part by entering MIDI data directly, drawing or step-inputting notes and controllers rather than performing it live, to drive virtual or hardware instruments.
fields.plain_english: MIDI programming means building a part by placing notes by hand instead of playing it. You add each note and its details on a grid.
fields.purpose_function: It exists so parts can be composed precisely without a live performance, which helps with tight drums, fast passages, or ideas the programmer cannot play in real time.
fields.practical_application: A producer step-enters a drum pattern and hi-hat rolls in the piano roll, then tweaks velocities so the programmed beat feels more human.
common_mistakes: Leaving every note at the same velocity, so the part sounds robotic.
Programming parts a real instrument could never play, which breaks the illusion.
Forgetting to set note lengths, so sustained parts sound choppy.
scenario_contexts: Building a drum beat from scratch in the piano roll.
Programming a fast synth arpeggio too quick to play by hand.
Laying out a bassline note by note for a demo.

sources: Sound on Sound (MIDI programming technique articles)

fields.definition: MIDI randomization is the application of controlled random variation to MIDI parameters such as timing, velocity, or note length, used to loosen mechanically precise data so programmed parts sound more natural, an effect often called humanizing.
fields.plain_english: MIDI randomization adds small random changes to things like timing or loudness. It stops programmed parts from sounding too perfect and machine-like.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to add back the subtle, natural unevenness of human playing to rigidly quantized or step-programmed MIDI, so parts feel less mechanical.
fields.practical_application: After quantizing a drum pattern, the engineer applies a small random offset to velocity and timing so the groove breathes instead of sounding stiff.
common_mistakes: Applying too much randomization, so timing sounds sloppy instead of natural.
Randomizing velocity on an instrument with velocity layers, which triggers unwanted sample changes.
Confusing randomization with quantizing, since one loosens timing and the other tightens it.
scenario_contexts: Humanizing a quantized hi-hat pattern.
Adding subtle velocity variation to a programmed piano part.
Loosening a stiff MIDI string section so it sounds more played.

sources: Steinberg Cubase Operation Manual (MIDI modifiers / randomize)
Sound on Sound (humanizing MIDI technique articles)
